In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel virulence factors involved in GBS pathogenesis.
the identification of new adhesins in the pathogenesis of meningitis caused by GBS.
the identification of the mechanisms used by the GBS ST‐17 clone, the leading cause of neonatal meningitis, to invade the host and cause disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the serine rich repeat protein Srr2, a cell surface anchored protein specific to the hypervirulent ST-17 GBS, has a dual role in the pathogenesis of meningitis, acting as a plasminogen/plasmin binding protein and as an adhesin for fibrinogen.
Srr2 contributes to the hypervirulent phenotype of GBS ST‐17 clone by binding to both fibringogen and plasmingogen.

Srr2, a novel multifaceted adhesion expressed by ST-17 hypervirulant GBS, is involved in binding to fibrinogen and to plasminogen, which contributes to bacterial survival in a murine GBS meningitis model.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ST‐17 hypovirulent clone uses Srr2 to bind to fibrinogen and to the fibrinolytic cascade, thereby contributing to its invasive potential.
the Srr2 adhesin of GBS ST‐17 clone contributes to meningitis by promoting the formation of bacterial clumps that are endocytosed and survive phagocytic clearance.

Srr2, a surface protein expressed by the GBS ‘hypervirulence’ ST‐17 strain, binds fibrinogen and, more importantly, plasminogen, which results in bacterial aggregates that are more efficiently phagocytosed and survive phagocytic clearance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ST‐17 GBS clone has acquired the ability to bind plasminogen, which contributes to its hypervirulent phenotype.

Srr2, a protein that is specific for the hypervirulent ST‐17 clone, is a multifacited adhesin that binds to fibrinogen and the fibrinolytic system and is involved in the formation of aggregates that are endocytosed and protected from killing.
GBS Srr adhesins are involved in binding to fibrinogen and to the host fibrinolytic pathway, and that this contributes to bacterial virulence.
